title: Differential Drive
description: Two independent wheels, no steering mechanism at all — and yet ARIA can go straight, turn, arc, or spin in place. Here's how two speeds are all it takes.

content.value: A car needs a separate steering mechanism to turn its front wheels. ARIA doesn't have one — she doesn't need it, because her two drive wheels can each spin at their own independent speed. That's the entire idea behind differential drive: steering isn't a separate system, it's just a difference between two wheel speeds.

left = right               ->  drives straight
left = right, but slower   ->  still straight, just slower
left > right                ->  arcs to the right
left = −right                ->  spins on the spot
one wheel = 0                ->  pivots around that wheel

content.title: 🕹️ Predict, then try it
content.hint: Before you touch a slider, guess what each combination above will do. Then check.

content.value: Four Combinations, All the Moves You Need

Notice there's no dedicated "turn" mechanism anywhere in ARIA's build — everything you just tried in the widget comes from nothing more than two independently-controlled motor speeds. That's the elegance of differential drive: maximum manoeuvrability from the simplest possible mechanism.

Formally, two numbers describe everything the robot is doing at any instant: its forward speed (the average of both wheels) and its turning rate (proportional to the difference between them). You don't need the formulas memorised — the widget's four rules above are the same idea in plain language.

This is also why differential drive robots can spin in a spot with zero turning radius, something a car fundamentally cannot do. It's a real advantage in tight spaces, and one reason it's such a common layout for small robots.
Key takeaway: differential drive steers with nothing but a difference between two independent wheel speeds. Equal speeds go straight; opposite speeds spin on the spot; anything between arcs.

quiz.question: You set the left wheel to 50 and the right wheel to 50. What does ARIA do?
quiz.explain: Equal wheel speeds mean no difference between them, so there's no turning rate — just straight travel.

quiz.question: You set the left wheel to 50 and the right wheel to -50. What happens?
options: It spins in place, since the wheels are pushing in opposite directions equally
quiz.explain: Opposite, equal-magnitude speeds cancel out forward motion entirely and produce pure rotation on the spot.

quiz.question: What's the one thing that makes differential drive so simple mechanically?
options: It needs a separate steering linkage like a car
Steering is just a difference between two independently-controlled wheel speeds — no extra mechanism needed
quiz.explain: No steering column, no linkage — turning comes entirely from software choosing two different speeds.
